metadata.title: Ninth Circuit rules states can regulate prediction markets as gambling

content.text:
The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Friday that states can regulate sports-related prediction market contracts as gambling, handing a major legal defeat to platforms including Kalshi, Crypto.com, and Robinhood.
The three judges, ruling without dissent, determined that Kalshi's sports event contracts did not qualify as "swaps" — the federally regulated derivative category the platforms had claimed — and instead constituted sports bets that states may govern under their gaming laws. "The substance of the sports event contracts offered on Kalshi's exchange is sports gambling, regardless of whether Kalshi calls them swaps," the court wrote in its opinion.
The ruling rejected requests for injunctive relief from Kalshi and Crypto.com, who had sought to block Nevada gaming regulators from halting their operations, according to CNBC. Robinhood, whose trading platform also features event contracts, was similarly denied relief.
Nevada's attorney general office welcomed the outcome as a confirmation of its position. "Sports betting does not become something else simply because a company calls it an 'event contract,'" deputy communications director Alcinia Whiters said in a statement.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction market platforms as federally licensed exchanges, pushed back on the ruling. A CFTC spokesperson said the court was wrong to conclude that sports-related event contracts fall outside the swap definition. "A derivative contract structured as a swap is a swap regardless of the underlying subject matter — the only exceptions in statute are onions and movie box office receipts," the spokesperson said in a statement. "The Ninth Circuit erred today when it invented a new and atextual exception" to the Commodity Exchange Act.
The decision creates a direct conflict with a ruling from the Third Circuit Court of Appeals, which sided with prediction market platforms earlier this year in blocking New Jersey's attempt to apply state gaming laws against them. A circuit split occurs when appellate courts in different parts of the country diverge on the same legal issue, a condition that historically draws Supreme Court attention, according to CNBC. "This is a classic circuit split," Columbia Law School professor Joshua Mitts told CNBC. "Ultimately, this is the kind of legal controversy which will make its way to the Supreme Court."
Federal judges throughout California, Arizona, and six additional states within the Ninth Circuit's jurisdiction are now bound by Friday's decision. Across the country, 44 states have taken the position that these platforms are offering sports betting rather than federally regulated financial products. The CFTC has sued at least nine states to block enforcement of state gambling laws against the platforms, and the agency has proposed new formal rules for prediction markets, establishing a review framework for sports-related event contracts.
Robinhood announced its intention to challenge the ruling. Neither Kalshi nor Crypto.com had offered a response when CNBC sought comment. DraftKings and Flutter Entertainment, FanDuel's parent company, each saw their shares climb — up 7% and more than 6%, respectively — after the ruling was issued.
